questions.q: Why does the lesson say a technically precise explanation (hallucination rate, BLEU-adjacent metric, confidence intervals) can still completely fail its audience?
options: It doesn't answer the question the listener actually has -- some version of 'should I be worried, and about what, specifically' -- even though every technical detail in it is accurate
Technical precision is always the wrong approach regardless of audience
The listener will always understand any sufficiently detailed technical explanation
Accuracy and effectiveness are the same thing in risk communication
questions.explain: Being technically correct doesn't guarantee the explanation is USABLE by someone without that technical background -- effectiveness requires translating the information into what the listener actually needs to decide something.

questions.q: What are the three components of the likelihood/impact/ask framework for explaining risk?
options: How often it happens (likelihood), what happens when it does (impact), and what decision you specifically want the listener to make (ask)
The engineer's name, the date of the meeting, and the project's budget
A list of every technical metric used to measure the system
The history of the company, its competitors, and its founding story
questions.explain: These three elements -- stated concretely -- are what let a non-technical listener actually understand and act on a risk, rather than just being informed that a risk exists in the abstract.

questions.q: In the 'well explained' version of the hallucination risk, what makes it more useful than 'there's some hallucination risk, but we think it's manageable'?
options: It gives a specific number (1 in 30), a concrete description of the failure, the current mitigation (human review), what changes under a proposed decision, and an explicit recommendation
It uses more complex technical vocabulary than the badly explained version
It is shorter than the badly explained version
It avoids giving the listener any specific number at all
questions.explain: The well-explained version gives every piece of information the listener actually needs to make a real decision -- a number, a mechanism, current mitigation, and what changes under the proposal -- not just a feeling of reassurance.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that 'we think it's manageable and we're monitoring it closely' is actually MORE risky to say than a specific, honestly-uncertain number?
options: If something later goes wrong, vague reassurance offers no paper trail or defense, while a specific stated estimate shows the risk was actually understood and knowingly accepted by the right people
Vague reassurance is always factually false, while specific numbers are always true
Saying a specific number is illegal in business risk communication
There is no real difference in risk between the two statements
questions.explain: If an incident happens later, 'we said it was manageable' provides no record of what was actually disclosed, while a specific number and its implications demonstrates the risk was genuinely quantified and consciously accepted.

questions.q: Why does a risk explanation that's missing the 'ask' component often result in nothing actually happening?
options: Without a specific decision being requested, the listener is informed but has no actual action or approval in front of them to act on
Listeners always ignore risk explanations regardless of whether an ask is included
The 'ask' component is purely optional and has no effect on outcomes
Missing an 'ask' always causes the listener to overreact instead of underreact
questions.explain: Information without a specific request for a decision leaves the listener with nothing concrete to approve, reject, or act on -- which is why the lesson treats the 'ask' as a required, not optional, part of the explanation.
